extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology / early-modern political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria for what counts as a Church, the grounds and limits of ecclesiastical authority, relations between Church and civil sovereign, and the offices of Christ as set out in an early-modern political-theological treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption prerequisite for Salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Salvation of a sinner, supposeth a precedent REDEMPTION; for he that is once guilty of Sin, is obnoxious to the Penalty of the same; and must pay (or some other for him) such Ransome, as he that is offended, and has him in his power, shall require.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ransome is required before Salvation; ransome is not to be understood as an equivalently-valued satisfaction that a sinner could claim, since sin cannot be removed by mere recompence. Sins may be pardoned gratis or upon a penalty God accepts; under the Old Testament God usually accepted sacrifice or oblation. Christ's sacrifice fulfilled the ransome God demanded (though not as an equivalent commercial satisfaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Church as God's House (metaphorical use)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sometimes (though not often) it is taken for Gods House, that is to say, for a Temple, wherein Christians assemble to perform holy duties publiquely.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a metaphorical sense (the congregation is meant), later used for the edifice itself to distinguish Christian temples from idolatrous ones (example citation: 1 Cor. 14.34). Greek Fathers called it Kuriake (The Lord's House).

rubrics_metrics.name: Church as Ecclesia — lawful congregation/assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Church (when not taken for a House) signifieth the same that Ecclesia signified in the Grecian Common-wealths; that is to say, a Congregation, or an Assembly of Citizens, called forth, to hear the Magistrate speak unto them…when they were called forth by lawfull Authority… it was Ecclesia Legitima.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes lawful (Ennomos Ecclesia) from tumultuous/seditious assemblies (Ecclesia Sugkechumene). The lawful character depends on being called by lawful authority; unlawful concourses produce only the particular acts of those present, not acts of the body corporate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church as body of all Christians (right to belong even if dispersed)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is taken also sometimes for the men that have right to be of the Congregation, though not actually assembled; that is to say, for the whole multitude of Christian men, how far soever they be dispersed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this sense the Church is a universal body of persons with a right to membership (example citation: Acts 8.3). This sense underlies statements like 'Christ is Head of the Church.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Church as part or the Elect (Church Triumphant)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sometimes, for the Elect onely; as (Ephes. 5.27.) 'A Glorious Church, without spot, or wrinkle, holy, and without blemish;' which is meant of the Church Triumphant, or, Church To Come.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word can denote the elect or the future perfected Church; usage varies with scriptural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the Church can be treated as one person (corporate agency requires lawful representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “And in this last sense only it is that the Church can be taken for one Person; that is to say, that it can be said to have power to will, to pronounce, to command, to be obeyed… For without authority from a lawfull Congregation, whatsoever act be done in a concourse of people, it is the particular act of every one of those that were present, and gave their aid … and not the act of them all in grosse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church is properly defined as 'A company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign; at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.' Acts claimed in the name of the Church require lawful authority; otherwise they are only individual acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal earthly Church; a commanding Church is equivalent to a civil commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is on Earth, no such universall Church as all Christians are bound to obey; because there is no power on Earth, to which all other Common-wealths are subject: There are Christians, in the Dominions of severall Princes and States… a Church, such as one as is capable to Command, to Judge, Absolve, Condemn, or do any other act, is the same thing with a Civil Common-wealth…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Church can command and enforce, it is identical with a civil commonwealth; therefore temporall and spirituall government are the same factually in this context. This denies the existence of a single supra-national Church with binding earthly authority over all Christians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a single chief pastor (unity of ecclesiastical authority under sovereign)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Doctors of the Church, are called Pastors; so also are Civill Soveraignes: But if Pastors be not subordinate one to another, so as that there may bee one chief Pastor, men will be taught contrary Doctrines… Who that one chief Pastor is… it is the Civill Soveraign.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid doctrinal faction and civil war there must be a single chief Pastor; the civil sovereign occupies this role by natural law and practice in a commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects without immediate revelation receive religious commands from their sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: “They to whom God hath not spoken immediately, are to receive the positive commandements of God, from their Soveraign; as the family and seed of Abraham did from Abraham their Father, and Lord, and Civill Soveraign.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External acts and professions of religion are obligations imposed by the civil sovereign on subjects who lack direct supernatural revelation. Internal thought and belief remain the province of conscience (God knows the heart) and are not subject to human enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private spirit or private revelation cannot override sovereign's religion; sovereign may punish dissenters
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was not unlawfull for Abraham, when any of his Subjects should pretend Private Vision, or Spirit, or other Revelation from God, for the countenancing of any doctrine which Abraham should forbid, or when they followed, or adhered to any such pretender, to punish them; and consequently that it is lawfull now for the Soveraign to punish any man that shall oppose his Private Spirit against the Laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private claims of revelation that contradict the sovereign's established religion are punishable; the sovereign enforces the religion of the commonwealth in externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler's authority grounded on consent and the people's promise
rubrics_metrics.description: “His authority therefore, as the authority of all other Princes, must be grounded on the Consent of the People, and their Promise to obey him. And so it was… 'speak thou with us, and we will hear'.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moses' authority depended on the people's belief in his sanctity and their promise to obey; more generally sovereign power is legitimized by consent and promise of obedience rather than solely by miraculous signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Scripture limited by sovereign bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: “None but the Soveraign in a Christian Common-wealth, can take notice what is, or what is not the Word of God… no man ought in the interpretation of the Scripture to proceed further then the bounds which are set by their severall Soveraigns.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripture may be read to learn and fear God, but making authoritative interpretations that challenge the sovereign's bounds or office is to 'gaze upon God irreverently.' The sovereign's representatives set the permissible interpretive limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy and spiritual gifts must be subordinate to sovereign's spirit/doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: “All Spirits Were Subordinate To The Spirit Of Moses… God came down in a cloud, and took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and gave it to the Seventy Elders… God endued them with a mind conformable, and subordinate to that of Moses… no Subject ought to pretend to Prophecy, or to the Spirit, in opposition to the doctrine established by him, whom God hath set in the place of Moses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prophetic gifts are recognized they are understood as delegated and subordinate to the sovereign's approved doctrine; independent prophetic claims in opposition are illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign power includes supreme authority over externals of worship
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whosoever had the Soveraignty of the Common-wealth amongst the Jews, the same had also the Supreme Authority in matter of Gods externall worship; and represented Gods Person…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Moses, the High Priest, the Kings of Israel) show civil or sacerdotal sovereigns exercising supreme power in matters of worship; after the people chose a king, the king held supremacy in religion and policy alike. The right remains even if practice varied or prophets checked misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold office of Christ and the temporal nature of his kingdom
rubrics_metrics.description: “We find in Holy Scripture three parts of the Office of the Messiah: the first of a Redeemer, or Saviour: The second of a Pastor, Counsellour, or Teacher… The third of a King, and Eternall King, but under his Father… Christs Kingdome Not Of This World.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christ acts as Redeemer (atoning sacrifice), Pastor/Teacher (conversion by himself and ministers), and future King (his temporal reign begins at general Resurrection). While believers by baptism are obliged to obey him as King when he takes the kingdom, his earthly bodily reign is not present now; his redemption was effected by his sacrificial death, which is described as both sacrificed and scape-goat imagery.
